the-murder-mystery-mindset.core: Live debugging interviews test method, not memorised fixes. Treat the broken system like a detective case: gather evidence, form hypotheses, test them one at a time and narrate your reasoning. Interviewers score a structured, hypothesis-driven approach above lucky guesses.

first_principles.problem: Candidates panic and randomly restart services, destroying evidence and learning nothing.
derivation: **Hypothesise** and test the most likely, cheapest first.

analogy.title: A detective at a crime scene
analogy.story: Don't move the body until you've photographed everything, then follow the evidence to the culprit.
analogy.breaks: Detectives can't re-run the crime; you can often reproduce the bug.

example.title: 'The website is slow'
flow: Ask: since when? all users? any deploys?

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Evidence-led path to the root cause.

check.q: Why avoid restarting a service immediately?
check.a: It may destroy the evidence (state, logs, stuck processes) needed to find the root cause.

the-first-60-seconds-vitals-check.core: Start every Linux investigation with a quick vitals sweep covering load, CPU, memory, disk, network and errors: uptime, dmesg | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 and top. In a minute you know which resource is saturated.

first_principles.problem: Candidates dive into application code when the box is out of disk or memory.
truths: A standard checklist prevents tunnel vision.
The USE method (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) covers resources.

analogy.title: A paramedic's ABC check
analogy.story: Airway, breathing, circulation, before any specialist diagnosis.
analogy.breaks: Patients show symptoms visibly; servers need commands to reveal them.

example.title: A slow box

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Disk full + memory pressure; OOM killer active.

code.text:
uptime            # load 24 on 8 cores
dmesg | tail      # Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (java)
free -m           # available 120 MB
df -h /           # 100% used

example.outcome: the saturated resource found in a minute.

check.q: What does high %wa (iowait) in vmstat suggest?
check.a: CPUs are idle waiting for disk I/O, pointing to a storage bottleneck.

strace-the-x-ray-machine.core: strace shows every system call a process makes (open, read, connect, futex…) with arguments, return values and timing. It reveals what a black-box program is actually doing: missing files, permission errors, hanging network calls or lock waits, without source code.

first_principles.problem: A process hangs with no logs and nobody knows why.
truths: Programs interact with the OS only via syscalls.
Errors appear as return codes like ENOENT or EACCES.
Blocking calls show where it's stuck.

analogy.title: An X-ray of a patient
analogy.story: You see the bones and the break without surgery.
analogy.breaks: X-rays are harmless-ish; strace can slow a busy process dramatically.

code.text:
strace -f -e trace=file ./app 2>&1 | grep -E 'ENOENT|EACCES'
# openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/app/config.yaml", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT

check.q: What does a process stuck in futex() usually indicate?
check.a: It's waiting on a lock or condition variable, often contention or deadlock between threads.

tcpdump-the-wire-tap.core: tcpdump captures packets on an interface with filters (host, port, protocol). It answers 'is traffic actually arriving, and what does it look like?': SYNs without SYN-ACKs, resets, retransmissions, DNS failures or TLS handshakes failing. It's ground truth below the application.

first_principles.problem: The app says the upstream is down; the upstream team says they never saw a request.
truths: Packets don't lie about what was sent.

analogy.title: A wiretap on a phone line
analogy.story: You hear exactly what was said and whether anyone picked up.
analogy.breaks: Encrypted calls hide content; TLS hides payloads, but handshake and flags remain visible.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: SYNs sent, no reply: firewall/security group dropping.

code.text:
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn host 10.0.4.12 and port 5432
# 10.0.1.5.41022 > 10.0.4.12.5432: Flags [S]
# 10.0.1.5.41022 > 10.0.4.12.5432: Flags [S]   (retransmit, no reply)

check.q: What does a repeated SYN with no SYN-ACK suggest?
check.a: Packets are being dropped (firewall, routing) or the host isn't reachable or listening.

reading-proc-the-kernels-live-dashboard.core: /proc is a virtual filesystem exposing live kernel and process state: /proc/<pid>/status (memory, threads), /proc/<pid>/fd (open files), /proc/<pid>/limits, /proc/<pid>/stack, /proc/meminfo, /proc/loadavg and /proc/net/tcp. Tools like ps and top read it, and you can read it directly when tools are missing.

first_principles.problem: A minimal container has no lsof or top, and a process is leaking file descriptors.

analogy.title: A car's diagnostic port
analogy.story: Plug in and read every sensor directly, even without the fancy dashboard.
analogy.breaks: Diagnostic ports are read-only; some /proc and /proc/sys entries are writable tunables.

example.title: Find an FD leak

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: 1,000 sockets to one host: connections never closed.

code.text:
ls /proc/4242/fd | wc -l          # 1019
grep 'open files' /proc/4242/limits   # 1024
ls -l /proc/4242/fd | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

example.outcome: leak diagnosed with only the kernel's own files.

check.q: How do you count a process's open file descriptors without lsof?
